pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–13 years

- **Topic:** Metals vs Non-Metals

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry 'The Periodic Table'):** The properties of metals and non-metals; the varying physical and chemical properties of different elements; the chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity; how patterns in reactions can be predicted with reference to the Periodic Table.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-1 / MS-PS1-2 supporting):** Use patterns in characteristic properties of substances to classify and identify materials.

- **Operational details:** Metals and non-metals are the great divide of the periodic table. Teach the cluster of PHYSICAL properties that typify metals — shiny (lustre), malleable/ductile, good conductors of heat and electricity, generally high melting points, mostly solid — versus non-metals (dull, brittle, poor conductors/insulators, lower melting points, many gases). Then the CHEMICAL signature: metals tend to form basic/alkaline oxides, non-metals form acidic oxides (the DfE 'oxides with respect to acidity' bullet); metals react by losing electrons. Tie the divide to POSITION: metals left/centre, non-metals upper right, with a staircase boundary and metalloids straddling it. Best taught by testing/sorting real property data rather than reciting lists, and by noting exceptions (mercury is a liquid metal; carbon/graphite conducts) so the pattern is a strong tendency, not an absolute rule.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal). The child classifies elements as metal/non-metal from property evidence, links the classification to periodic-table position, and states one chemical difference (e.g. metal oxides basic vs non-metal oxides acidic).
bestPractices: Teach metal/non-metal as a CLUSTER of co-occurring properties, not a single trait.
Have pupils classify from property EVIDENCE (test/sort data) rather than memorised lists.
Add the chemical signature: metal oxides tend to be basic, non-metal oxides acidic.
Link the classification to periodic-table POSITION (metals left/centre, non-metals upper right).
Use exceptions (mercury liquid, graphite conducts, metalloids) to teach that it's a strong tendency, not an absolute.
keyRepresentations: A test-and-sort bench (conductivity, malleability, lustre, oxide pH)
A results table feeding a metal/non-metal classification
A periodic table shaded by the metal/non-metal divide with a staircase boundary
commonMisconceptions: All metals are magnetic (only iron/nickel/cobalt are).
All metals are hard and solid (mercury is liquid; some are soft).
Any shiny material is a metal (lustre alone is not sufficient).
Metal and non-metal oxides behave the same in water (they differ in acidity).

learn.summary: Learners classify elements as metals or non-metals from a cluster of co-occurring property evidence (conductivity, malleability, lustre, oxide acidity), link that classification to periodic-table position (metals left/centre, non-metals upper right with a staircase boundary), and state a chemical difference (metal oxides tend to be basic, non-metal oxides tend to be acidic). Exceptions (liquid mercury, conducting graphite, metalloids) teach that the divide is a strong tendency, not an absolute rule. Age 11–13.

activities.title: Test-and-sort bench: metal or not?
feedback: If the learner classifies from one property alone, point to a conflicting case: a shiny plastic strip looks lustrous but won't conduct — ask them to gather the other test results before deciding.

When graphite (a non-metal) conducts, acknowledge the surprise and have them check malleability and oxide behaviour too. It is brittle and flaky rather than malleable, and its oxide (carbon dioxide) is acidic, so the full cluster still places it as a non-metal even though it has a grey sheen. Conduction alone isn't decisive.

When mercury classifies as a metal despite being liquid, confirm: state varies, but its conduction and lustre (and metallic bonding) still mark its metallic character — malleability simply can't be shown for a liquid, so it isn't the deciding test here.
After sorting, prompt: 'Where did the basic-oxide samples end up on the table, and where did the acidic-oxide ones?' to make the position–chemistry link explicit.
activities.rationale: The divide is learned by testing and sorting property data rather than reciting lists; actively generating a results table and seeing clusters fall onto table position makes the property cluster and its link to position a discovery, and the included exceptions frame the pattern as a tendency.
sourceClaims: Characteristic properties are used to classify and identify substances (NGSS PS1.A patterns)
Metal oxides are generally basic and non-metal oxides acidic; the metal/non-metal divide has metalloid/exception cases (Hg liquid, graphite conducts)
DfE KS3 Chemistry: properties of metals and non-metals; chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity; predicting patterns from the periodic table
learnerActions: Take each solid element sample and run quick tests: touch it to a circuit (does the bulb light?), tap it with a hammer (does it flatten or shatter?), and check its shine (lustrous or dull?). Then, for elements whose oxide dissolves in water, test a simulated or teacher-prepared oxide solution with universal indicator (acidic or basic?). Mercury is only simulated or shown by the teacher in a sealed sample, never hammered or burned.
Record each result in a results table, one row per element.
As evidence accumulates, place each sample onto a metal or non-metal map overlaid on the periodic table, and watch where the two clusters land.
Work through puzzle cases — liquid mercury and conducting graphite — and decide how to classify them despite one odd property.
State one chemical difference between the two classes: metal oxides tend to be basic/alkaline, non-metal oxides tend to be acidic (a strong pattern, not a guarantee for every oxide).
activities.intendedInsight: Metals and non-metals are distinguished by a CLUSTER of co-occurring properties, not one trait. The shiny, malleable, conducting, basic-oxide elements pool on the left/centre of the periodic table and the dull, brittle, insulating, acidic-oxide elements on the upper right. The staircase divide broadly matches the metal/non-metal split, with metalloids along it and hydrogen (a non-metal placed top left) as a notable exception.

activities.title: Shaded periodic table reference
feedback: If a learner reads the boundary as a hard line, point to the metalloids straddling the staircase as intermediate cases.
When predicting from position, ask them to name at least two expected properties, not one, to reinforce the cluster idea.
activities.rationale: A shaded reference and tap-to-reveal chart consolidate the position–property link and serve as a companion to active testing; as a reference tool it supports recall and prediction but does not itself let the learner generate the test evidence, so it is best paired after bench work.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Chemistry: properties of metals and non-metals; chemical properties of metal and non-metal oxides with respect to acidity; predicting patterns from the periodic table
learnerActions: Study a periodic table shaded by the metal/non-metal divide, with the staircase boundary and metalloids straddling it marked.
Use a tap-to-reveal comparison chart with a metals column and a non-metals column; tap a property (e.g. malleability, conductivity, oxide acidity) to highlight which side shows it.
Given a new element's position, predict whether it is likely a metal or non-metal and which properties you'd expect.
activities.intendedInsight: Periodic-table position predicts metal/non-metal character and its associated property cluster; the boundary is a staircase with metalloids in between, so it is a graded divide rather than a hard line.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: does a magnet define a metal?
feedback: If the learner predicts all metals stick, use the observation (only iron sticks) to show magnetism is a property of a few metals, not the definition — copper, aluminium and gold also don't stick yet are metals.
If they refuse to call mercury a metal because it is liquid, note that sodium is soft and mercury liquid; state and hardness vary, while conduction, lustre and metallic bonding still unite them.
If they call the shiny plastic a metal, have them check conduction — the plastic won't conduct, the metals will; use the cluster, not one cue.

Full-credit reasoning rejects 'magnetic = metal' and 'shiny = metal' and cites conduction and malleability, correctly handling non-magnetic copper, liquid mercury and shiny plastic; a partial response lists metallic properties but cannot say which property settles a given object or link uses to properties.
activities.rationale: Counterexamples (non-magnetic copper, liquid mercury, shiny plastic) discriminate a learner using a defining property cluster from one leaning on a single misleading cue, directly targeting the common misconceptions that all metals are magnetic, all metals are hard solids, and anything shiny is a metal.
learnerActions: Lay out copper, aluminium, iron and a shiny plastic strip; the teacher presents a sealed/demonstrated sample of liquid mercury (never pupil-handled). Before testing, predict which a magnet will pick up and explain WHY.
Test with a magnet and observe: only the iron sticks (copper, aluminium and mercury do not, and the plastic is not a metal).
Explain the gap between prediction and result, then give two other tests (conductivity, malleability) that show copper IS a metal despite not being magnetic.
Decide whether the demonstrated liquid mercury is a metal, and whether a shiny sweet wrapper is really metal or just shiny plastic, saying which test settles each.

Answer: where on the periodic table would you look to predict whether an element is a metal, and why are metals chosen for saucepan bases versus electrical wires — which property does the work each time?
activities.intendedInsight: Magnetism and shine are single misleading cues; metals are identified by a coherent cluster (conductivity, malleability where state allows, lustre, mostly high melting points, left/centre periodic position). Only iron, nickel and cobalt are commonly magnetic; shiny plastic is not a metal; and liquid mercury is still a metal.

constraints: The shaded periodic table and tap-to-reveal chart are reference scaffolds: they support prediction and recall but do not let the learner generate the test evidence that produces a classification, so pair them after hands-on (or simulated) testing rather than as a substitute.

The metal/non-metal divide is a strong tendency, not an absolute rule — always include exceptions (mercury is a liquid metal; carbon/graphite conducts; metalloids straddle the boundary) so learners don't over-apply any single property.

No single property defines a metal: magnetism (only iron/nickel/cobalt commonly), shine, hardness or solidity each fail alone. Require a cluster — conduction and malleability (where state allows) are the most decisive.

Oxide acidity depends on the element and conditions, and some metal oxides are insoluble; teach 'metal oxides tend to be basic, non-metal oxides tend to be acidic' as a strong general pattern tested on soluble/pre-prepared oxides, not as a guarantee for every case.

Recognition/matching tasks (categorisation, oxide-acidity multiple choice) assess alignment but do not by themselves elicit the independent evidence-gathering of bench testing; use them to consolidate after active classification.

If run as a real lab rather than the designed interactive, the burn-and-test-oxide step and any mercury require teacher supervision and safe setup — pre-prepared/soluble oxide samples and a sealed, teacher-demonstrated mercury sample (never pupil-handled) for ages 11–13.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The recommended medium was a 2d interactive (simulated bench); if delivered physically, combustion and reactive/hot materials and the mercury counterexample are hazardous and need teacher supervision, safe setup, soluble/pre-prepared oxide samples and a sealed demonstrated mercury sample. The source did not specify safety handling; flagged for review.

The oxide-acidity test is a KS3 simplification: many metal oxides are insoluble and will not register on aqueous universal indicator, so the step is reliable only for oxides that dissolve; retained as a tendency, not a universal demonstration.
Two of three cited sources (NGSS, RSC) were marked verified:false in the source row; comparative efficacy or necessity of any one format is not established by the sources and is not asserted here.

The legacy entry rated 3D and conversation formats 'poor' and asserted a dialogue 'cannot supply the test results'; this has been softened to a narrowly scoped affordance note (reference/recognition tools don't generate the learner's own evidence) rather than a universal claim about medium superiority.

The original separated two element sets (a magnet poeTask with copper/aluminium/iron/plastic and a diagnostic prompt that showed mercury); these are merged into one coherent PoE in which mercury is a teacher demonstration, so the mercury feedback has a referent without requiring pupil handling.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: lay out copper, aluminium, iron and a shiny plastic strip. Ask the child to predict which a magnet will pick up and WHY. A 'metal = magnetic' model predicts all the metals stick. Only the iron does. The pre-observation prediction and reasoning expose whether magnetism is being used as the definition of metal.
probeDeeper: Copper isn't magnetic — give me two other tests that show it IS a metal.
Where on the periodic table would you look to predict whether an element is a metal?
Why are metals chosen for saucepan bases and electrical wires — which property is doing the work each time?
A shiny sweet wrapper: how would you decide if it's really metal or just shiny plastic?
assess.correctAnswer: The rule is wrong. Most magnets only stick to iron, nickel and cobalt — most metals (copper, gold, aluminium) aren't magnetic — and shininess alone isn't enough (shiny plastic isn't a metal; mercury is a liquid metal). Metals are better identified by a CLUSTER of properties: good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable/ductile, lustrous, mostly high melting points, and their position on the left/centre of the periodic table. Full marks reject 'magnetic = metal' and give conduction/malleability.

errorPatterns.pattern: all metals are magnetic ('if a magnet sticks, it's metal; if not, it isn't')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test copper, aluminium, gold with a magnet — none stick, all are metals. Only iron/nickel/cobalt are magnetic. Magnetism is a property of a few metals, not the definition.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — if a magnet sticks it's a metal, and metals are always magnetic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: classifies copper/aluminium as non-metal because a magnet won't stick, or expects every metal to be magnetic

errorPatterns.pattern: all metals are hard solids ('metals are always solid and strong')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mercury is a liquid metal; sodium is soft enough to cut. State (and hardness) vary; conduction and metallic bonding are what unite them.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — mercury can't be a metal because metals are always hard and solid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: refuses to call mercury a metal because it's liquid, or equates 'metal' with 'hard'

errorPatterns.pattern: shiny = metal ('anything shiny is a metal')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lustre is one clue but not sufficient — test conduction: the plastic won't conduct, the metals will. Use the property cluster, not one cue.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes for shine — the shiny bag would count as metal too.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: calls the shiny plastic bag a metal, or treats lustre as sufficient on its own

responseLevels.gap: Relies on a single cue (magnetism or shine); misclassifies copper, mercury or shiny plastic accordingly.
responseLevels.full: Identifies metals by a coherent cluster (conductivity, malleability, lustre, periodic-table position), correctly handles non-magnetic metals, liquid mercury and shiny non-metals, and matches each real-world use to the property doing the work.
responseLevels.partial: Rejects the magnet rule and lists metallic properties, but treats them as a memorised list — can't say WHICH property to use for a given object or link uses to properties.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A friend says 'you can always tell a metal because it's shiny and a magnet sticks to it.' I show you mercury (a shiny liquid metal), copper (a metal a magnet does NOT stick to), and a shiny plastic gift bag. Is your friend's rule right? Then the important part: explain what really makes something a metal.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The counterexamples (non-magnetic copper, liquid mercury, shiny plastic) split a child who identifies metals by a defining cluster (especially conductivity and malleability) from one leaning on a single misleading cue (magnetism or shine). Only the former handles all three objects correctly.
